newsitem.title: GERMANY: FORECAST - EMU worries to depress mark.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - EMU worries to depress mark.

text.p: Fears about European economic and monetary union and relatively sluggish German growth promise to leave the mark weaker against major currencies over the next two years, a Reuter survey published on Wednesday showed.

According to a survey of 28 economists who closely follow the German economy, the mark is likely to fall to 1.5519 against the dollar by the third quarter of 1998 from 1.5330 now and will slip to 70.00 against the yen from 71.98.
"The mark is going down, down, down," said Holger Schmieding, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
He and others said that fears about EMU are the major reason for worry about the mark.

According to their arguments, the currency to replace the mark, the Euro, will not be as stable as the German currency because European governments do not share Germany's determination to keep inflation down and budgets under control.
That means investors will shy away from German securities over the next few years for fear of taking a stake in a less stable currency than the historically strong mark.
"In the run-up to monetary union, the mark will not be the powerful currency that we have seen in recent years," said Craig Shute, economist at Bear Stearns in London.
In addition to the dark EMU cloud hanging over the German currency, economists also see economic fundamentals suggesting a weaker German currency.
The German economy, they say, will grow less quickly than the U.S. and Japan's, meaning interest rates in those countries may climb, making investment opportunities there more attractive.
The survey showed economists expect the mark will stand at 1.5320 against the dollar at the end of 1996 and at 71.98 against the yen.

There was a wide range of forecasts for the mark's movements against the dollar. DKB International expected the German currency to slip all the way to 1.80 while MM Warburg expected the mark to remain fairly steady at 1.35.
Against the yen, DKB International saw the mark falling to 65.50 while Bayerischen Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank saw the German currency at 75.00.
Against the British pound economists saw the mark on average at 2.3800 by the end of the third quarter of 1998 compared with 2.4495 now.
